sentences.text: Paris, 1988.
Thousands of passengers arrived at Charles de Gaulle Airport, collected their luggage, and continued their journeys.
But one man stayed.
His name was Mehran Karimi Nasseri.
And for the next eighteen years, this airport would become his home.
His story would one day inspire a Hollywood film.
The real one is quieter, sadder, and far less certain.

Thousands of passengers arrived at Charles
de Gaulle Airport, collected their
luggage, and continued their journeys.
But one man stayed.
His name was Mehran Karimi Nasseri.

And for the next eighteen years, this
airport would become his home.

His story would one day inspire a
Hollywood film.

The real one is quieter, sadder, and far
less certain.

sentences.text: Nasseri was born in Iran, most likely in 1945, in the oil town of Masjed Soleyman.
Much of what we know about his early life comes from his own telling, and his telling changed over the years.
He said he had studied in England in the 1970s.
He said he had been expelled from Iran in 1977, after protesting against the Shah.
At different times, he said his mother was Scottish, or Swedish. Neither claim was ever confirmed.
Journalists who later looked into his past questioned parts of that account.
What is better documented is this: in 1981, he was recognized as a refugee in Belgium.
For several years, he lived there, and travelled in Europe.

What is better documented is this: in

For several years, he lived there, and

sentences.text: Then, in 1988, he set out for Britain.
What happened next depends on whose account you read.
In the version most often reported, his passport and his refugee certificate were stolen along the way.
In other versions, he sent the papers away himself.
Either way, he arrived in England without them.
British officials refused him entry and returned him to the airport he had flown from: Charles de Gaulle.
In France, he now had a problem with no simple solution.
He could not prove who he was.
And so, in August 1988, a man without papers sat down in Terminal 1.

segments.chapter: How an airport became his home

sentences.text: It is often said that he was trapped in a sealed transit zone.
That is not quite right.
Reports place him in a public area of the terminal, where travellers, cleaners and police walked past him every day.
He was not locked in.
What held him in place was paperwork.
Weeks became months.
Months became years.
His case moved slowly between lawyers, officials and governments.
And as it did, a bench in Terminal 1 became an address.
“Eventually, I will leave the airport,” he told The Associated Press in 1999. “But I am still waiting for a passport or transit visa.”

sentences.text: His routine was precise.
He washed and shaved every day.
He kept his belongings close: a luggage trolley, boxes and bags, stacked carefully beside a red plastic bench.
He read newspapers and magazines.
He studied economics.
And he wrote, every day, in a diary he kept for years.
Airport workers came to know him well.
Some brought him food. Some brought him newspapers.
The airport doctor gave him paper to write on.
To them, he became a familiar figure, and he took on a new name: Sir Alfred.

sentences.text: By the 1990s, the man on the bench had become a story.
Journalists from around the world came to Terminal 1 to interview him.
Photographers made his portrait among the passengers and departure boards.
His story inspired a French film, Lost in Transit, and an English opera, Flight.
He answered questions politely, and patiently.
In 2004, a journalist writing for The Guardian spent time with him, and found that key parts of the story he told could not be confirmed.
But the more he was asked about his past, the less settled that past became.

sentences.text: In 2004, the story reached Hollywood.
Steven Spielberg's film The Terminal starred Tom Hanks as Viktor Navorski, a traveller stranded at a New York airport.
The film was not a biography.
It moved the story to America and invented its own hero.
But DreamWorks had acquired the rights to Nasseri's story, for a sum widely reported at around $250,000.
The same year, his memoir, The Terminal Man, was published under the name Sir Alfred Mehran.
A man who owned almost nothing now had a film deal, a book, and a famous address.

sentences.text: The strangest part of the story is what happened next.
In the mid-1990s, Belgium indicated he could return there.
Later, France offered him papers that would have allowed him to stay.
He refused to sign them.
According to reports, the documents identified him as Iranian, under his original name.
He wanted to be recognized differently: as Sir Alfred, and as British.
So the man who had waited years for papers turned down the ones he was offered.
Those who befriended him said the years in the terminal took a toll. In the 1990s, the airport doctor described him as “fossilized here.”
What began as a legal problem had become, at least in part, a choice.

sentences.text: In the summer of 2006, after nearly eighteen years, he fell ill and was taken to hospital.
His corner of Terminal 1 was cleared.
When he was discharged, he did not go back to the airport.
Reports say he later lived in a shelter in Paris.
Accounts of the years that followed are sparse, and they do not always agree.
For the first time since 1988, Sir Alfred was no longer living in the terminal.

sentences.text: Sixteen years later, he came back.
In September 2022, according to the airport, he returned to live in a public area of Charles de Gaulle.
On 12 November, around midday, he suffered a heart attack in Terminal 2F.
He died there, of natural causes, according to the airport.
He was in his late seventies.

sentences.text: Airports are built for movement.
Millions of people pass through them, and almost no one stays.
Mehran Karimi Nasseri stayed.
Part of his story was a failure of paperwork, and part of it may always remain his own.
He came to Charles de Gaulle as a man without documents, and he is remembered as the traveller who never really left.
